sbh3.2:1.6: *Vicinoti* → *pravicinoti* → *parivitarkayati* → *parimīmāṁsām āpadyate* — the same four *prajñā*-function verbs that appear throughout the Śrāvakabhūmi. The progression moves from coarse to fine inquiry: general examination → close discrimination → deliberation → thorough critical examination. The accumulation conveys that *vipaśyanā* is sustained, multi-aspected investigation rather than a single act of looking.
sbh3.2:2.5: *Yāvad-bhāvikatā* and *yathāvad-bhāvikatā* — 'as-far-as-it-goes-ness' and 'as-it-actually-is-ness.' A key Yogācāra distinction running throughout the *vipaśyanā* method. The first asks the *scope* of the object; the second its *nature*.
sbh3.2:3.18: The three gateways are stages in the maturation of an investigation, not three separate practices. First the topic is held loosely (sign-only). Then actively worked (seeking). Then rested in the conclusion (reviewing). The *asamāhita* qualifier on stage one is striking — initial holding doesn't yet require absorbed attention.
sbh3.2:5.9: *Svalakṣaṇa* / *sāmānya-lakṣaṇa* — what makes *this* thing *this* (the particular nature), and what is shared across many things (typically *anitya*, *duḥkha*, *anātman*). Insight in the classical sense usually arises from general-characteristic contemplation.
sbh3.2:5.36: The proof-establishing-reasoning move deploys the three pramāṇas — testimony, inference, perception — with the specific test 'is there a self here?' The Buddhist anti-ātman investigation framed as a pramāṇa exercise.
sbh3.2:5.37: *Dharmatā-yukti* is the limit of inquiry: at some point one rests in the nature-of-things and stops further analysis (*na cintayati, na vikalpayati*). The contemplation has reached its proper terminus.
sbh3.2:9.8: The root prints *aśruvedanām upādāya*, but the body-fluid sequence and parallels in sbh2.2/sbh2.5 support expected *aśru-svedam* ('tears and sweat'). The English marks this as a conjectural/corrupt repair rather than silently turning *vedanā* into lymph.
sbh3.2:11.18: The skeleton-sign passage distinguishes actual and non-actual signs. The non-actual category includes painted or fabricated skeletons, here represented as made from stone, wood, or grass/reed. The point is not four coordinate signs, but two sign-types: actual skeleton versus constructed/imagined skeleton.
sbh3.2:11.20: Asanga acknowledges that practitioners often work with painted images, carved skeletons, or imagined skeletons rather than actual corpses. He distinguishes the practice with imagined material (yields the *deha-śaṅkalikā* sign — the schematic body-form) from practice with an actual seen skeleton (yields the *asthi-śaṅkalikā* sign — the specific bone). Both are valid; they produce different signs.
sbh3.2:12.6: An elegant taxonomic move. The cemetery sequence is grouped by what causes the change: early stages (decay through bloating) happen by the body's own internal processes; middle stages (gnawing through scattering) happen by external agents; the bone stages reflect both. Unattractiveness is not just 'the body falls apart' but 'the body changes by itself, by what acts on it, and by both together.'
sbh3.2:13.4: The insight move. Specific-characteristic investigation gave the body's gross unattractiveness in detail. General-characteristic investigation collapses the difference between the seemingly-fair and the obviously-unattractive: same nature, same property, same outcome. The fair color-form one finds attractive *now* is the same kind of thing as the corpse one would recoil from.
sbh3.2:14.3: The dark-side reflection turns on a conditional: if the practitioner fails to know the unattractiveness of fair color-form as it actually is and generates craving for it, that craving is mere perversion on the dark side. The point is not that he 'generates unattractiveness,' but that he fails to recognize the unattractiveness already present in what appears fair.
sbh3.2:14.5: *Niḥsaraṇadharmaḥ saduḥkhaḥ...* is not 'escape-by-suffering.' In context, the dark-side perversion is painful and dangerous, yet not final: it is a condition from which escape is possible through seeing unattractiveness as it is.
sbh3.2:16.4: The printed *kaṇḍavara* is likely a corrupt/extracted form of *kaḍevara/kalevara* ('body, corpse'). The earlier rendering as 'itching and scratching' followed *kaṇḍū* semantics from elsewhere and is not supported by this reasoning passage, which reduces fair/unattractive designation to mere form/body.
sbh3.2:17.6: Asanga gives the practitioner an explicit experimental protocol: 'as I cultivate unattractiveness, sensual craving doesn't arise; when arisen, it goes away.' The practice is verified pragmatically by its effect on the defilement — a precise statement of how a contemplative claim is to be tested.
sbh3.2:17.10: The proof-establishing reasoning includes an inferential check: an object opposed to a defilement should not produce that defilement. The previous wording made the line sound affirmative, as if defilement arises through the counter-object; the Sanskrit is rhetorical and supports the antidote logic.
sbh3.2:17.16: *Prahāṇa-pratipakṣa* means an antidote for abandoning the target defilement, not an antidote opposed to abandonment itself. The line restates the practice-function already given at 17.1 and 17.5.
sbh3.2:21.21: The printed *māṣamātra* ('bean-measure') is contextually implausible after *akṣarāṇy etāni ravanti* and *śabdamātram*. The English marks a conjectural/corrupt repair to the expected reduction of abuse to mere sounds/syllables.
sbh3.2:21.27: The Sanskrit *anitya, ete 'pi sparśā ye te apakārakās te 'py anityāḥ* anchors the equanimity argument in impermanence. Three reasoning moves toward universal *maitrī*: speech-act analysis (abuse is mere syllables, body is mere elements, contacts arise and pass); universal-suffering recognition (all beings suffer; adding to suffering is unbecoming); long-saṁsāric-time argument.
sbh3.2:22.7: The printed root has *tasmān na sarvasattveṣu samacittatā*, with a negation that conflicts with the immediately following instruction to cultivate equality-view and equal benefit/happiness aspiration. The English follows the contextually required affirmative and marks the line conjectural/corrupt.
sbh3.2:25.6: The reasoning-investigation collapses *maitrī* into *anātman*. Even lovingkindness practice is to be done with full recognition that there is no self sending the *maitrī* and no self receiving it — only aggregates conditioned by *karma* and *kleśa*. The Yogācāra distinctive: *maitrī* is not at odds with emptiness; the deepest *maitrī* is *maitrī* informed by *anātman*.
sbh3.2:58.1: Closing colophon for the entire Yogasthāna III. The Sanskrit accusative *tṛtīyaṁ yogasthānaṁ samāptam* is the standard Yogācāra chapter-closing formula. The English is rendered into the bracketed shape used for the parallel Yog I colophon at sbh1.3:86.1.
sbh3.2:26.1: Parallel to the maitrī treatment at 24-25, this paragraph applies the four-yukti vipaśyanā schema to *idaṁ-pratyayatā pratītyasamutpāda* — dependent-origination as a meditation object. The four yuktis (*apekṣā*, *kāryakāraṇa*, *upapatti-sādhana*, *dharmatā*) are the canonical Yogācāra analytical engines. The PS treatment is the longest of the four vipaśyanā treatments and unfolds the twelve-link doctrine (*dvādaśa-bhavāṅga*) in terms of the four characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* / *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) and the twofold cause-result structure (*ākṣepaka-hetu* / *abhinirvarttaka-hetu*).
sbh3.2:27.1: Vipaśyanā on *dhātuprabheda* (the distinction of the six elements) — shorter than the PS treatment because the element framework is already familiar from sbh2.5. The six elements (earth, water, fire, wind, space, consciousness) are analyzed via own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general-characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*); the body is shown to be merely conventional like 'house' (composed of elements + space).
sbh3.2:28.1: Vipaśyanā on *ānāpānasmṛti* (mindfulness of breathing) — the fifth and last of the carita-viśodhana practices. Treated here as a *vipaśyanā* object (not, as in sbh2.6, as a *śamatha* base): the breath is investigated under the four yuktis with respect to its impermanence, dependent arising, and conventional designation. The closing remark — that breath-mindfulness conduces to the cutting of *vitarka* — anchors the practice in its canonical anti-discursive function.
sbh3.2:29.1: Transition from the carita-viśodhana ālambana treatments (paragraphs 20-28 — maitrī, PS, dhātu, breath) into the śamatha-vipaśyanā framework. The reciprocal-dependence formula here — 'vipaśyanā purified by śamatha; śamatha amplified by vipaśyanā' — is one of the load-bearing claims of Yogācāra meditation theory, and recurs at the close of this section (38.1-39.8) as the *yuganaddha-mārga*.
sbh3.2:30.1: The 9-fold *prayogatā* schema — nine kinds of engagement on the bright-side, nine kinds (inverse) on the dark-side, yielding the 18-fold prayoga total. The nine are: anurūpa (conformable), abhyasta (practiced), aśithila (non-slack), aviparīta (unperverted), kāla (time), upalakṣaṇa (observation), asaṁtuṣṭa (dissatisfaction), avidhura (undisturbing), samyak (right). This is the standard Yogācāra typology of how a practitioner engages śamatha-vipaśyanā well or poorly.
sbh3.2:31.6: *śamatha* is defined here as 'the ninefold mental abiding' (*navākārā cittasthitiḥ*), pointing to the nine-stage taxonomy in detail at sbh3.1 (cittasthāpana through samādhāna). The four-mode/three-door definition of vipaśyanā at 31.14 has its fuller treatment at the start of sbh3.2.
sbh3.2:34.5: The five-fold *vibhāvanā* (vivid-realization) — by inward sign-contraction, by non-attention-from-non-mindfulness, by attention to something else, by attention to the antidote, and by attention to the signless element — is the technical engine of right-engagement (*samyak-prayogatā*). Each mode targets a different way the mind drifts: scatter, sign-grasping, fixation, opposing-defilements, and clinging to signs respectively.
sbh3.2:35.12: The painter simile is a classic Yogācāra image for the progressive purification of *adhimokṣa* through repeated cycles of resolve-and-erase. Like the painter, the meditator does not improve by repainting the same flawed image on top of itself (*na janvandhasya tadrūpakapariśuddhiṁ nigacchet*) but by erasing and remaking again and again.
sbh3.2:36.1: *Āvaraṇa-viśuddhi* — purification from the four obstacles. The Yogācāra fourfold obstacle-typology (*paritamanā, nivaraṇa, vitarka, ātmasaṁpragraha*) maps to: dispiritedness with practice, the five hindrances, defiled discursive thought, and self-conceit-from-attainment. The fourfold investigation (own-nature, cause, danger, antidote) is the Yogācāra standard for treating any unwholesome dharma.
sbh3.2:39.1: *Yuganaddha-vāhin* (going-yoked) marks the convergence of śamatha and vipaśyanā into a single path-stream. This is the fulfillment of the framework introduced at the start of this section (29.3-4). The same yuganaddha doctrine grounds the *adhiprajñā-dharma-vipaśyanā* of the supramundane path. Compare AN 4.170 (Yuganaddha Sutta) for the canonical Pali parallel.
sbh3.2:40.1: *Anantar-uddāna* — 'subsequent uddāna,' an intermediate summary verse following a major section. This uddāna covers the 9-fold prayoga + āvaraṇa-viśuddhi material in śloka-meter. The verse is corrupt in places (esp. the line about pakṣa/kāla); meaning is recoverable from the prose discussion above.
sbh3.2:41.1: The four-fold *manaskāra* framework — *cittasaṁtāpana* (mind-heating), *cittābhiṣyandana* (mind-suffusing), *praśrabdhi-janaka* (serenity-producing), and *jñāna-darśana-viśodhana* (knowledge-and-vision-purifying) — is the Yogācāra operational protocol for getting an *ādikarmika* (beginner) into one-pointedness and delight-in-abandonment. Each manaskāra targets a specific phase: heating produces *saṁvega*; suffusing produces *praharṣa*; the serenity-producing transitions into śamatha; the knowledge-purifying transitions into vipaśyanā. The same fourfold reappears in sbh4.1 as the framework underlying the seven attentions.
sbh3.2:42.3: The four *saṁvejanīya-sthāna* — places that generate urgency — pair across two axes: *one's own / others'*, and *misfortune at hand (present) / fortune past (gone)*. The wise-attention to misfortune face-to-face heats the mind; the wise-attention to past-fortune-now-perished also heats it (through impermanence). This is one of the tightest Yogācāra schemas for the practical generation of *saṁvega*.
sbh3.2:42.7: The three bases of gladdening: *Three Jewels recollection* (the standard fourfold formula: Buddha, dharma, fellow brahmacāris, the auspicious-death), *śikṣāpada-pāriśuddhi* (recollection of purity of trainings), and *ātmani viśeṣādhigama-saṁbhāvanā* (the non-shrinking confidence in one's own capacity for distinctive attainment). Each is developed at length in 42.8 through 44.2.
sbh3.2:45.1: The gold-smith simile — one of the more famous Yogācāra meditation similes. The yogī is the smith; the mind is the raw metal; the four manaskāras together produce the *workable* mental state in which śamatha and vipaśyanā can be 'shaped' to the practitioner's purpose. The simile recurs in the *Yogācārabhūmi* and the *Mahāyāna-sūtrālaṅkāra*.
sbh3.2:46.4: The five *nimitta-grahaṇa* sequence: (1) *saṁvejanīya* (urgency), (2) *prasadanīya* (gladdening), (3) *ādīnava* (danger), (4) *āloka* (luminous), (5) *vasturūpaṇa* (substance-image). The yogajña (teacher) leads the beginner through each in order. Each *nimitta* is an internal object the practitioner cultivates to ground a specific manaskāra and prepare for śamatha-vipaśyanā. The lust-conducted student (here) is led specifically into the *aśubhā* practice; later paragraphs cover the maitrī-, idaṁ-pratyayatā-, dhātu-, and ānāpāna-conducted variants.
sbh3.2:47.5: The 'volition-less arising' principle — central to Yogācāra meditation psychology. Non-regret, joy, gladness, and mind-delight should not be *willed* into being; they arise *by the nature of things* (*dharmatā*) once the prior condition (pure virtue → non-regret → joy → gladness → mind-delight) is in place. The chain is: pure śīla → avipratisāra → prāmodya → praharṣa → prīti-manaskatā. Each step is dharmatā-arising, not effortful production.
sbh3.2:48.5: The threefold sign-system the yogī presents to the ādikarmika: (1) saṁvejanīya (urgency) was the *aśubhā* application of the four saṁvejanīya-sthāna; (2) prasadanīya (gladdening) was the recollection of Three Jewels + śīla + ātmano-adhigama-saṁbhāvanā; (3) ādīnava (danger) is the three-fold analysis of how signs / vitarka / defilements harm the mind. Following these, the *āloka-nimitta* (luminous-sign) is given in paragraph 49 and the *vasturūpaṇa-nimitta* (substance-image) implicitly governs the entire engagement with the meditation object.
sbh3.2:50.2: The *janapadakalyāṇī* (country-beauty) parable — a canonical Pali parallel exists at SN 47.20 *Janapadakalyāṇī Sutta*. Asaṅga gives the *yogācāra* allegorical reading: country-beauty = defilement-obsessions; great gathering = ten signs; oil-vessel = śamatha-bound mind; sword-raised executioner = the danger-sign just taken up. The parable enacts the *satyābhyavaṣṭabdha-prayogatā* (anchored-engagement) introduced at the start of the 9-fold prayoga framework.
sbh3.2:51.6: The multiplication-sequence from one corpse to immeasurable corpses — a Yogācāra elaboration of the Pali *aśubhā* meditation. Each step of the resolve (*adhimokṣa*) extends the imagined object outward until 'all directions and intermediate-directions' are filled without gap. The result-sign is a luminous (*prabhāsvara*) resolve in which real-attention (*bhūta-manaskāra*) follows. Same multiplication-pattern is used for maitrī (54.6) and other practices.
sbh3.2:52.6: The 36 *aśuci-dravya* — the 36 unattractive substances of the body, taken as the *aśubhā* basis. From this base, the four foundations of mindfulness are established in turn: (1) body-as-body inwardly (own body, 52.7); (2) body-as-body externally (others, 52.8-9); (3) inwardly-and-externally (52.10-11); (4) feelings/mind/dharmas through the four formless aggregates analyzed in the three modes (śamatha/distraction/vipaśyanā) (52.12-19). This is the practical-instruction synthesis of *aśubhā* (the carita-viśodhana practice at sbh2.2) with the four foundations of mindfulness (the framework developed at sbh2.0 ¶¶68-88).
sbh3.2:53.1: The alms-round and four-postures protocol — extending mindfulness through the post-sitting routine. The five elements (53.1-7) — alms-round behavior, lodging avoidances, faculty-restraint, food-moderation, speech-discipline — together form the standard Yogācāra prescription for *non-relinquishment of the object* in daily activity. Compare the parallel treatment of *jāgarikā-anuyoga* (sbh1.3 ¶42) and *saṁprajāna-vihāritā* (sbh1.3 ¶¶43-47).
sbh3.2:54.4: The friend-enemy-neutral system in *maitrī* is the standard Yogācāra elaboration of the Pali *brahmavihāra*. The three parties model the practitioner's reactive structure: friends evoke easy maitrī (no obstacle); enemies evoke the obstacle of resistance; neutrals evoke the obstacle of indifference. Cultivating equal maitrī across the three trains the mind to produce *maitrī* regardless of object-class — the prerequisite for the immeasurable-extension.
sbh3.2:56.13: *Samanaskāra* — the ādikarmika-yogī who has obtained attention. This is the structural milestone that the entire ādikarmika-tutorial has been preparing for. The English keeps the Sanskrit term because of its technical specificity: *sa-manaskāra* literally 'one-possessing-attention,' marking the transition from pre-attention preparation into the concentrated-stage proper. The signs at 56.15-22 are the diagnostic markers — limited but observable body-serenity, swift-onset śamatha, weakened defilement-arising, alms-round attention preserved. From this point the practitioner is ready for the seven attentions of sbh4.1.
sbh3.2:11.1: The full enumeration of the body's bone-categories — hand, foot, knee, thigh, upper arm, forearm, spine, backbone, jaw, teeth-row, skull. This is the *prima materia* of the *asthi-śaṅkalikā* (skeleton-perception) practice. The pre-existing JSON skipped from `vikṣiptakam ityadhimucyate` directly to `api ca dve śaṅkalike` (PDF 5190), dropping the enumeration and the *anuvyañjana-grāhī* vs. *mere-nimitta-grāhī* distinction that grounds it.
